feed.subtitle: A simple, whitespace theme for academics. Based on [*folio](https://github.com/bogoli/-folio) design.

entry.title: Sample Blog Post
entry.content:
Note: please use the table of contents as defined in the front matter rather than the traditional markdown styling.

Equations

This theme supports rendering beautiful math in inline and display modes using MathJax 3 engine. You just need to surround your math expression with $$, like $$ E = mc^2 $$. If you leave it inside a paragraph, it will produce an inline expression, just like \(E = mc^2\).

To use display mode, again surround your expression with $$ and place it as a separate paragraph. Here is an example:

\[\left( \sum_{k=1}^n a_k b_k \right)^2 \leq \left( \sum_{k=1}^n a_k^2 \right) \left( \sum_{k=1}^n b_k^2 \right)\]

Note that MathJax 3 is a major re-write of MathJax that brought a significant improvement to the loading and rendering speed, which is now on par with KaTeX.

Images and Figures

Its generally a better idea to avoid linking to images hosted elsewhere - links can break and you might face losing important information in your blog post. To include images in your submission in this way, you must do something like the following:

{% include figure.liquid path="assets/img/2027-04-30-distill-example/iclr.png" class="img-fluid" %}

which results in the following image:

To ensure that there are no namespace conflicts, you must save your asset to your unique directory /assets/img/2027-04-30-[SUBMISSION NAME] within your submission.

Please avoid using the direct markdown method of embedding images; they may not be properly resized. Some more complex ways to load images (note the different styles of the shapes/shadows):

A simple, elegant caption looks good between image rows, after each row, or doesn't have to be there at all.

Interactive Figures

Here’s how you could embed interactive figures that have been exported as HTML files. Note that we will be using plotly for this demo, but anything built off of HTML should work (no extra javascript is allowed!). All that’s required is for you to export your figure into HTML format, and make sure that the file exists in the assets/html/[SUBMISSION NAME]/ directory in this repository’s root directory. To embed it into any page, simply insert the following code anywhere into your page.

{% include [FIGURE_NAME].html %}

For example, the following code can be used to generate the figure underneath it.

import pandas as pd
import plotly.express as px

df = pd.read_csv('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/plotly/datasets/master/earthquakes-23k.csv')

fig = px.density_mapbox(
    df, lat='Latitude', lon='Longitude', z='Magnitude', radius=10,
    center=dict(lat=0, lon=180), zoom=0, mapbox_style="stamen-terrain")
fig.show()

fig.write_html('./assets/html/2027-04-30-distill-example/plotly_demo_1.html')

And then include it with the following:


<div class="l-page">
  <iframe
    src="{{ 'assets/html/2027-04-30-distill-example/plotly_demo_1.html' | relative_url }}"
    frameborder="0"
    scrolling="no"
    height="600px"
    width="100%"
  ></iframe>
</div>

Voila!

Citations

Citations are then used in the article body with the <d-cite> tag. The key attribute is a reference to the id provided in the bibliography. The key attribute can take multiple ids, separated by commas.

The citation is presented inline like this: (a number that displays more information on hover). If you have an appendix, a bibliography is automatically created and populated in it.

Distill chose a numerical inline citation style to improve readability of citation dense articles and because many of the benefits of longer citations are obviated by displaying more information on hover. However, we consider it good style to mention author last names if you discuss something at length and it fits into the flow well — the authors are human and it’s nice for them to have the community associate them with their work.

Footnotes

Just wrap the text you would like to show up in a footnote in a <d-footnote> tag. The number of the footnote will be automatically generated.This will become a hoverable footnote.

Code Blocks

This theme implements a built-in Jekyll feature, the use of Rouge, for syntax highlighting. It supports more than 100 languages. This example is in C++. All you have to do is wrap your code in a liquid tag:

{% highlight c++ linenos %}
code code code
{% endhighlight %}

The keyword linenos triggers display of line numbers. You can try toggling it on or off yourself below:

Diagrams

This theme supports generating various diagrams from a text description using mermaid.js directly. Below, we generate examples of such diagrams using mermaid syntax.

Note: To enable mermaid diagrams, you need to add the following to your post’s front matter:

mermaid:
  enabled: true
  zoomable: true # optional, for zoomable diagrams

The diagram below was generated by the following code:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant John
    participant Alice
    Alice->>John: Hello John, how are you?
    John-->>Alice: Great!
```

sequenceDiagram
    participant John
    participant Alice
    Alice->>John: Hello John, how are you?
    John-->>Alice: Great!

Tweets

An example of displaying a tweet:

There was a 'Moved Permanently' error fetching URL: 'https://twitter.com/rubygems/status/518821243320287232'

An example of pulling from a timeline:

There was a 'Moved Permanently' error fetching URL: 'https://twitter.com/jekyllrb'

For more details on using the plugin visit: jekyll-twitter-plugin

Blockquotes

We do not grow absolutely, chronologically. We grow sometimes in one dimension, and not in another, unevenly. We grow partially. We are relative. We are mature in one realm, childish in another. —Anais Nin

Layouts

The main text column is referred to as the body. It is the assumed layout of any direct descendants of the d-article element.

.l-body

For images you want to display a little larger, try .l-page:

.l-page

All of these have an outset variant if you want to poke out from the body text a little bit. For instance:

.l-body-outset

.l-page-outset

Occasionally you’ll want to use the full browser width. For this, use .l-screen. You can also inset the element a little from the edge of the browser by using the inset variant.

.l-screen

.l-screen-inset

The final layout is for marginalia, asides, and footnotes. It does not interrupt the normal flow of .l-body-sized text except on mobile screen sizes.

.l-gutter

Other Typography?

Emphasis, aka italics, with asterisks (*asterisks*) or underscores (_underscores_).

Strong emphasis, aka bold, with asterisks or underscores.

Combined emphasis with asterisks and underscores.

Strikethrough uses two tildes. Scratch this.

  1. First ordered list item
  2. Another item
  • Unordered sub-list.
  1. Actual numbers don’t matter, just that it’s a number
    1. Ordered sub-list

  2. And another item.

    You can have properly indented paragraphs within list items. Notice the blank line above, and the leading spaces (at least one, but we’ll use three here to also align the raw Markdown).

    To have a line break without a paragraph, you will need to use two trailing spaces. Note that this line is separate, but within the same paragraph. (This is contrary to the typical GFM line break behavior, where trailing spaces are not required.)

  • Unordered lists can use asterisks

  • Or minuses

  • Or pluses

I’m an inline-style link

I’m an inline-style link with title

I’m a reference-style link

I’m a relative reference to a repository file

You can use numbers for reference-style link definitions

Or leave it empty and use the link text itself.

URLs and URLs in angle brackets will automatically get turned into links. http://www.example.com or http://www.example.com and sometimes example.com (but not on Github, for example).

Some text to show that the reference links can follow later.

Here’s our logo (hover to see the title text):

Inline-style:

Reference-style:

Inline code has back-ticks around it.

var s = "JavaScript syntax highlighting";
alert(s);

s = "Python syntax highlighting"
print(s)

No language indicated, so no syntax highlighting.
But let's throw in a <b>tag</b>.

Colons can be used to align columns.

Tables Are Cool
col 3 is right-aligned $1600
col 2 is centered $12
zebra stripes are neat $1

There must be at least 3 dashes separating each header cell. The outer pipes (|) are optional, and you don’t need to make the raw Markdown line up prettily. You can also use inline Markdown.

Markdown Less Pretty
Still renders nicely
1 2 3

Blockquotes are very handy in email to emulate reply text. This line is part of the same quote.

Quote break.

This is a very long line that will still be quoted properly when it wraps. Oh boy let’s keep writing to make sure this is long enough to actually wrap for everyone. Oh, you can put Markdown into a blockquote.

Here’s a line for us to start with.

This line is separated from the one above by two newlines, so it will be a separate paragraph.

This line is also a separate paragraph, but… This line is only separated by a single newline, so it’s a separate line in the same paragraph.

entry.title: Does Recursion Depth Mean Difficulty? A Token-Level Test of Mixture-of-Recursions

link.title: Does Recursion Depth Mean Difficulty? A Token-Level Test of Mixture-of-Recursions

entry.content:
The question

Mixture-of-Recursions (MoR) runs one shared Transformer block a different number of times for different tokens. The token visualisations in the paper show some words receiving one pass and others receiving three. Section 5.2 of the paper states that recursion depth “directly indicates how easily the next token can be predicted within the given context”.

The paper supports this statement with examples. We found no per-token comparison of depth with a measure of difficulty in the main text or Appendix I of the paper. This post makes that comparison on the authors’ released checkpoints and held-out data. We assume familiarity with the standard Transformer and do not assume any background in Mixture-of-Experts or adaptive computation.

This post reports four findings.

  • Depth is low for easy tokens and stops rising near the median token. The rank correlation with difficulty is 0.10 to 0.22.
  • The hardest tenth of tokens gain the least from depth under three recursions.
  • Token identity alone explains 35% to 44% of expert-choice depth and 99.5% of token-choice depth.
  • The router still matters. Random routing at the same depth split raises loss, and full depth for every token does not lower it.

These results suggest that depth reflects a learned allocation of computation more than a measure of difficulty.

How MoR assigns depth

A recursive Transformer applies a shared block up to \(N_r\) times. Weight sharing across depth with per-position halting appears in earlier work, including Adaptive Computation Time and Universal Transformers . Mixture-of-Depths added top-\(k\) token selection to skip layers. MoR combines a shared block with a router trained from scratch and a matching key-value cache design. Mixture-of-Experts chooses which weights process a token, whereas MoR chooses how many times the same weights run.

Figure 1 shows the two router types in MoR.

Figure 1. The two routers, drawn with nine illustrative tokens. A green cell marks a token processed at that recursion.

The expert-choice router follows Zhou et al. . At each recursion, a top-\(k\) selection keeps a fixed share of the tokens in the sequence. With three recursions the shares are 1, 2/3 and 1/3, so each depth holds a third of the tokens in every sequence. Depth under this fixed split is a rank within the sequence, and a hard document cannot receive more depth than an easy document. The top-\(k\) selection also uses the whole sequence, including future tokens, and the paper calls this effect information leakage.

The token-choice router assigns each token one depth before the first recursion. This router is causal, but the number of tokens at each depth can differ. Uneven load leaves hardware idle because a batch waits for its deepest tokens, so training includes a balancing loss. On our data the three depths hold 46.6%, 28.9% and 24.5% of tokens.

Neither router receives a difficulty label. Both routers are trained with the language modelling loss and routing losses, so any link between depth and difficulty arises during training.

The test

Models and data. We used the released 360M checkpoints: expert-choice with 2, 3 and 4 recursions, token-choice with 3 recursions, and the vanilla model without recursion. The data is the first 1,000 sequences of 2,048 tokens from the authors’ held-out FineWeb set. Position \(t\) predicts token \(t+1\), so every per-token value below refers to that prediction.

Difficulty. The main challenge is that language tokens have no ground-truth difficulty. We used the vanilla model’s per-token loss as a proxy, because that model has no router and cannot share MoR’s routing decisions. We also report its predictive entropy. Both measure difficulty for one model of this size, so a token may be hard here and easy for a larger model.

Benefit. We define the benefit of depth at a position as the loss in nats with nearly every token forced to depth 1 minus the loss with every token forced to full depth, using the same MoR model.The code keeps at least one token per recursion, so the depth 1 run leaves one token per sequence at full depth.

Routing swaps. We replaced only the top-\(k\) selection and kept the router’s own gate values:

def topk(scores, k, policy):
    if policy == "router":
        return torch.topk(scores, k, dim=1)
    rank = -scores if policy == "inverted" else torch.rand_like(scores)
    index = torch.topk(rank, k, dim=1).indices
    return torch.gather(scores, 1, index), index

Pre-set rules. We wrote the expert-choice analysis and three reading rules before seeing results. The thresholds are our own choices.Depth tracks difficulty if the mean per-sequence Spearman correlation with vanilla loss is at least 0.2 and at least 0.1 after removing token and position effects. Depth is mainly lexical if the held-out coefficient of determination (R²) on token identity is at least 0.5. Routing matters if random routing is worse with a confidence interval that excludes zero. The choices of 1,000 sequences and 64 position bins are also arbitrary. The token-choice run, the decile views and the token lists came afterwards and are exploratory.

Check against the paper. Our losses for the vanilla, 3-recursion and 2-recursion models are 2.761, 2.773 and 2.731. Table 3 of the paper reports a negative log-likelihood (NLL) of 2.7824, 2.7925 and 2.7511 for matching models. Our three values are each about 0.02 lower, which is consistent with a sample of the same test set. All confidence intervals are 95% bootstrap intervals over sequences. Each interval for a correlation lies within 0.01 of the mean.

Depth rises for easy tokens, then stays flat

Figure 2 shows the first test sequence, which is the default sample in the official routing notebook. The sequence contains the word “defensively”, and the paper uses the same subword as an example.

Figure 2. One test passage under the 3-recursion expert-choice model. Hover or tab to a token to read its depth and the vanilla loss on the next token.

The paper describes “-ensively” as straightforward to predict and therefore needing fewer steps. In this passage, the router assigns depth 1 to the position that predicts this subword. The vanilla loss at that position is 5.16 nats, which is in the hardest fifth of tokens. A single token is not evidence of a trend, so the table below uses all two million positions.

Model Correlation with vanilla loss Correlation with vanilla entropy Vanilla loss at each depth, shallow to deep
Expert-choice, 2 recursions 0.098 0.088 2.61, 2.91
Expert-choice, 3 recursions 0.217 0.249 1.90, 3.47, 2.91
Expert-choice, 4 recursions 0.197 0.216 1.80, 3.08, 3.39, 2.77

The correlations are positive and weak. Under our pre-set rule, the 3-recursion model passes narrowly, the 4-recursion model misses by 0.003, and the 2-recursion model fails. A rank correlation of 0.22 corresponds to about 5% of rank variance, so the size of the correlation matters more than the pass or fail.

With 3 and 4 recursions, tokens at depth 1 are easy, but the highest mean loss is at a middle depth and the deepest group is easier than that middle group.

Figure 3. Left: mean depth by decile of vanilla loss, on the full depth scale. Right: loss reduction from full depth by the same deciles, for 3 recursions.

Mean depth rises through the easiest three or four deciles and then stays nearly flat. With 3 recursions, mean depth moves from 1.45 to 2.07 by the fourth decile and ends at 2.11 in the hardest decile. In the hardest decile, 32% of tokens receive depth 3, which is close to the one third expected if depth ignored difficulty, and 21% receive depth 1. The statement in the paper fits the easiest deciles and does not describe the tokens above the median.

The hardest tokens gain least

Difficulty measures how poorly a model predicts a token, and benefit measures how much full depth reduces the loss on that token. The right panel of Figure 3 shows the benefit by loss decile. With 3 recursions, benefit peaks at 0.29 nats in decile 7 and falls to 0.05 in decile 10. The drop also appears with 2 recursions (0.18 to -0.02) and with 4 recursions (0.40 to 0.19). The end-of-text token has a mean depth of 1.00 across 2,074 occurrences, and the vanilla loss on the following token is 6.52 nats. The preceding context contains little information about how a new document begins. One plausible reading is that some loss comes from missing information, which repeated computation cannot add.

Benefit also rises with assigned depth. With 3 recursions, tokens at depths 1, 2 and 3 gain 0.02, 0.25 and 0.38 nats. The rank correlation between depth and benefit is about 0.2 for all three models, so this link is also weak. The Limits section explains why this trend requires caution.

Token identity explains much of depth

We fitted the mean depth of each token on half of the sequences and predicted depth on the other half.

Figure 4. Share of depth variance on held-out sequences explained by token identity alone.

Figure 4 shows the held-out R² for each model. For expert-choice models, R² is below our 0.5 threshold for calling depth mainly lexical. With 3 recursions, the most common depth of a token matches its actual depth 72% of the time, against 33% for the largest depth group.

Among the 350 token types with at least 500 occurrences, the deepest include “ who”, “ human”, “ could” and “ get”. Their mean vanilla losses are 2.7 to 3.8 nats. The shallowest include “ don”, “ United” and “ al”, which have predictable continuations, and also “ But” (4.15 nats), which does not.

Expert-choice depth also depends on context. After removal of token and position effects, the correlation with vanilla loss remains 0.13 to 0.16, and the correlation with entropy remains 0.19 to 0.26. The routers at later recursions receive hidden states that have passed through the shared block, so context can affect the decision.

Token-choice routing is close to a lookup table

The token-choice router makes one decision, after a single Transformer layer. Token identity explains 99.5% of depth on held-out sequences, and the most common depth of a token matches its actual depth 99.9% of the time. The correlation with vanilla loss is -0.095 and changes to -0.005 after removal of token and position effects. Depth in this checkpoint contains almost no information about context.

Shuffling the router’s choices within each sequence raises loss from 2.90 to 5.34. Forcing every token to depth 3 raises it to 6.02, and forcing depth 1 raises it to 4.72. Extra recursions raise the loss on tokens assigned to shallower depths, which suggests that each token type is processed at a fixed depth. Table 3 of the paper reports a higher NLL for token-choice than for expert-choice (2.9163 against 2.7925). The lookup behaviour may contribute to this gap, but we have not tested that explanation.

The router still matters

Figure 5 shows the added loss when the trained router is replaced at inference.

Figure 5. Added loss for expert-choice models. The depth split is fixed for the random and inverted runs.

Random routing adds 0.074 to 0.124 nats, and inverted routing adds 0.121 to 0.138 nats, with intervals that exclude zero. Table 13 of the paper gives related evidence, with an NLL of 2.9335 for a model trained with random routing against 2.8667 for the best learned router in that table. Our swap changes only inference, so part of our gap may come from the mismatch with training.

Full depth for every token adds 0.0003 to 0.0044 nats. With 3 recursions, the router uses two thirds of the block applications and matches the loss at full depth. The efficiency case for MoR rests on this result and does not depend on depth being a measure of difficulty.

How to read a depth map

Depth maps invite the same interpretation as attention maps, and Jain and Wallace showed that attention weights require testing before being read as explanations. We suggest four checks for any adaptive-depth model, each of which requires only inference.

  1. Correlate depth with per-token loss from a separate model, and plot depth by loss decile, because the correlation alone does not show the plateau reported here.
  2. Report how much of depth a token-identity baseline explains.
  3. Measure benefit as well as difficulty, because the two diverge for the hardest tokens.
  4. Swap the router at a fixed depth split to separate router quality from the amount of computation.

Depth under fixed capacity is a rank within a sequence, so depth values cannot be compared across documents.

Limits

  • One training run per setting. Our intervals cover variation across sequences, not across training seeds.
  • One dataset and one model size. We tested 360M models on educational web text. Larger models or other domains may differ.
  • Difficulty is a proxy. Vanilla loss describes one model and is not a property of the token.
  • Forced runs are off-distribution. The models never trained with random, inverted or forced routing, so those losses combine router quality with mismatch. The token-choice forced runs are too far from training to give a usable benefit measure, so we do not report one.
  • Benefit is partly circular. Tokens routed deep during training are the ones the shared block learned to refine, so their larger benefit may be a result of routing and not a reason for it.
  • Future tokens. Expert-choice results use whole-sequence top-\(k\), as the official evaluation does. Depth during token-by-token decoding may differ.
  • Exploratory results. The token-choice, decile and token-list results came after the pre-set analysis.
  • Variants not tested. We did not run the key-value sharing checkpoint.

Reproducing this work. All routing runs for one checkpoint take about four minutes on one A100 GPU and do not require training or a cluster scheduler. The relevant official files are expert_choice_router.py and token_choice_router.py. We did not edit these files; a wrapper replaces the top-\(k\) call at run time. We will release our scripts after review.
entry.summary: Mixture-of-Recursions gives each token a recursion depth, and the original paper reads depth as a sign of how easily the next token can be predicted. We test that reading on the released 360M checkpoints. Depth is low for easy tokens and stops rising near the median token, the hardest tokens gain least from depth, and token-choice depth is almost a fixed function of the token.

entry.content:
Why batch-one TTS is a launch-overhead problem

A voice agent sits there until the slowest model in the cascade spits out its first token. For text-to-speech (TTS), I keep staring at two numbers. Time to first chunk (TTFC) is how long before any audio can play. The real-time factor (RTF) is compute time per second of audio, and it has to stay well below 1 for gap-free streaming.

Codec-language-model TTS turns both into a decoding problem. Qwen3-TTS-12Hz emits one 16-codebook codec frame per 80 ms of audio. A 28-layer talker transformer predicts codebook 0, and a 5-layer code predictor fills codebooks 1–15, one autoregressive step at a time. At batch size one, every one of those steps is a small memory-bound matrix-vector product. You mostly pay for the gaps between launches. Persistent megakernels fuse a whole forward pass into one launch, which is why people built them for LLM decoding .

So, can a megakernel someone hand-tuned for a text model actually help a speech model, if I don’t write a new kernel?

Three facts that make reuse possible

I started from an open-source megakernel for Qwen3-0.6B decoding , itself derived from MegaQwen . It runs 128 persistent blocks of 512 threads with in-kernel grid barriers and reaches about 1,000 tokens/s on an RTX 5090.

Three fairly boring facts made the reuse possible.

  1. Same shape. The Qwen3-TTS talker has the same backbone as Qwen3-0.6B : hidden size 1,024, 28 layers, 16 query and 8 KV heads of dimension 128, and MLP width 3,072. Only the vocabulary (3,072 codec ids), an untied output head, and the RoPE base differ. The vocabulary is a build constant, and RoPE tables come from the host.
  2. Depth is a runtime argument. The kernel loops for layer in 0..num_layers, with num_layers passed at launch. The 5-layer code predictor has the same per-layer shape, so the same compiled binary runs it with num_layers=5.
  3. A tiny input hook. TTS decode steps take a sum of 16 codebook embeddings plus a text embedding, so there is no single token id. A three-line expression makes a negative id read a pre-written buffer instead of the embedding table, at the kernel’s two entry points. Including an #ifndef guard for the vocabulary size, the entire kernel diff is 14 added and 6 removed lines in a ~1,600-line file, comments included.
const __nv_bfloat16 *embed_row =
  (input_token_id >= 0) ? embed_weight + input_token_id * HIDDEN_SIZE
                        : hidden_buffer;

Results on one RTX 5090

Metric Result Target
TTFC, first complete codec frame 50.5 ms < 90 ms
TTFC, streaming, mean of 3 runs 81.6 ms < 90 ms
TTFC, streaming, all runs and text lengths 78–98 ms < 90 ms
RTF, non-streaming / streaming 0.175 / 0.234 < 0.3
Code predictor, PyTorch 179 ms/frame (RTF ≥ 2.24) -
Code predictor, reused megakernel 9.8 ms greedy (18×) / 10.9 ms sampled (16.4×) -

Batch size 1, bf16, CUDA 12.8, PyTorch 2.7+. Timings use perf_counter with torch.cuda.synchronize() and exclude warm-up. The baseline RTF comes from the predictor alone (179 ms per 80 ms frame), so it is a lower bound. Some streaming runs went over 90 ms.

The code predictor is what blew the RTF budget. Fifteen dependent steps per frame, and each of those steps was about 70 small PyTorch launches. Once that loop ran on the reused kernel, RTF went from at least 2.24 down to 0.175.

Where the time goes

Steady-state compute per 80 ms frame (≈15 ms). The code predictor's 15 sequential launches still dominate.

Time to the first frame: tokenize 2.3 ms, embedding build 7.2 ms, prefill (8 single-token steps) 24.9 ms, first talker step 3.1 ms, and first code-predictor pass 13.0 ms, for 50.5 ms total.

Most of the latency win came from ordinary engineering

Streaming TTFC after each change (log scale). Intermediate values are approximate single measurements.

The first streaming number I wrote down was 35,932 ms. Getting it down from there was mostly unglamorous engineering:

  • A list became a generator (about 1,096 ms).
  • Warming up the vocoder removed an 834 ms first call (about 192 ms).
  • Warming up the sampling path, not just argmax, removed a 107 ms first predictor call (about 92 ms).
  • Batching and caching constant embeddings brought it to 81.6 ms.

That’s about 440× if you stay inside the streaming measurement. Stack that same 35,932 ms baseline against the 50.5 ms first-frame number and you can quote 711×, but the two clocks don’t share a boundary. I would not lead with 711×.

What the quality checks show

I scored the five released audio samples on a CPU with Whisper large-v3 , UTMOS , and TorchAudio-Squim . I had no reference-implementation audio, so these are absolute numbers.

Sample WER UTMOS (trimmed) Non-speech tail before trimming
short (5 words) 0.20 3.19 2.7 s
e2e test (10 words) 0.40 3.54 0.5 s
medium / long / streaming demo n/a (input text not saved) 3.62 / 4.00 / 3.67 12.8 / 21.8 / 27.0 s

short (5 words)

e2e test (10 words)

medium

long

streaming demo

UTMOS is measured on copies trimmed after generation to the end of speech (VAD, 250 ms margin, fade-out). Whole-file UTMOS on the raw files is 1.42–3.58.

Whatever speech is actually in the file sounds okay. Two problems are still sitting there.

  • Spurious syllables get inserted (“Hello Cher, how are you today?”). Pooled WER is 5/15 on the two known texts, or 3/15 if you don’t count Whisper writing “megakernel” as “mega kernel”.
  • The model doesn’t stop. Generation runs to a word-count frame cap, leaving up to 27 s of low-level non-speech, where UTMOS drops to about 1.2–1.5.

I can point at two shortcuts that would explain this. I still haven’t run the ablation that would tell me which one, so I’m guessing. One is that the kernel implements 1-D RoPE , while the talker is configured for multimodal RoPE (sections [24, 20, 20]) . Second, the official generation code suppresses certain special tokens and this implementation doesn’t. Either way, end-of-speech isn’t reliably emitted.

When does this transfer

I got away with the reuse because a few conditions happened to line up:

  • The auxiliary transformer has the same per-layer shape as the main one.
  • Depth is a runtime argument, not a template parameter.
  • Everything that differs (input embedding, vocabulary-specific heads, RoPE tables) lives outside the fused layer loop.

If the shapes differ, you need a second build. If the positional scheme differs inside attention, as here, reuse is fast but not exact. Reuse also leaves the sequential structure untouched: 15 dependent predictor launches per frame and 8 single-token prefill steps remain the next targets.

Takeaways

Before you sit down to write a new kernel, check whether the shapes already match. A text-LLM megakernel might already cover the stages in a speech model.

In this pipeline, warming up the first call and fixing the generator plumbing moved the needle more than the kernel did. Warming up argmax does not warm up sampling. I found that out the annoying way.

Latency is the easy number to brag about. This pipeline hits its latency targets and still doesn’t know when to stop talking.

entry.title: a post with marimo snippets
entry.content:
marimo notebooks can run Python directly in the reader’s browser. Opt a page in from its front matter:

---
layout: post
title: a post with marimo snippets
marimo: true
---

Nothing is loaded on pages without that flag, so bundling the plugin costs nothing site-wide.

Runnable snippets

Wrap fenced Python blocks in a container and the runtime turns them into an interactive notebook after the page loads:

import marimo as mo

slider = mo.ui.slider(1, 20, value=5, label="n")
slider

mo.md(f"The first {slider.value} squares: {[i**2 for i in range(1, slider.value + 1)]}")

Until the runtime has moved those blocks into place the container stays hidden, so readers never see the raw source flash before it becomes a notebook.

Embedding a hosted notebook

If you already publish a notebook — on marimo.app or your own WASM host — embed it instead:

{% al_marimo_embed src="https://marimo.app/l/your-notebook" height="700px" caption="Sampling demo" %}

The frame is sandboxed without allow-same-origin, so the embedded notebook cannot reach this page’s storage or cookies.

A note on what this loads

The marimo-snippets runtime is vendored into the plugin at a pinned version and served from your own site, rather than pulled from a CDN — so no third-party origin executes script in your readers’ pages. Running a notebook does contact marimo’s host, which is worth knowing before you opt a page in.
entry.summary: running Python in the browser with marimo

entry.title: یک نوشتهٔ راست‌چین
entry.content:
این نوشته نمونه‌ای از پشتیبانی زبان‌های راست‌چین در al-folio است. کافی است در front matter صفحه، lang را روی یکی از زبان‌های راست‌چین بگذارید:

---
layout: post
title: عنوان نوشته
lang: fa
---

افزونهٔ al_rtl صفت dir="rtl" را روی عنصر <html> قرار می‌دهد. چون این صفت روی ریشهٔ سند است، نوار ناوبری، پاورقی و جای نوار پیمایش هم درست می‌شوند — نه فقط متن اصلی.

زبان‌های شناخته‌شده به‌صورت پیش‌فرض: عربی، عبری، فارسی، اردو، پشتو، کردی، سندی، اویغوری، دیوهی و چند زبان دیگر. برای تغییر این فهرست:

al_rtl:
  langs: [fa, ar]

کد و ریاضیات چپ‌چین می‌مانند

کد و فرمول‌ها بدون توجه به زبان متن، چپ‌چین باقی می‌مانند. اگر جهت آن‌ها راست‌چین می‌شد، ترتیب عملگرها و نقطه‌گذاری به‌هم می‌ریخت:

def normalize(code):
    return code.strip().lower().split("-")[0]

فرمول‌ها هم همین‌طور: \(E = mc^2\) و در حالت نمایشی:

\[\left( \sum_{k=1}^n a_k b_k \right)^2 \leq \left( \sum_{k=1}^n a_k^2 \right) \left( \sum_{k=1}^n b_k^2 \right)\]

متن انگلیسی درون یک جملهٔ فارسی، مثل The quick brown fox، به‌درستی نمایش داده می‌شود، چون مرورگر خودش الگوریتم دوجهته را اعمال می‌کند.
